section_summary: This section consists of State Department records from November 1931 through August 1940 concerning the Japanese language, focusing on romanization systems, educational materials, and consular administration. A central theme is the Japanese Government's promulgation of Cabinet Order No. 3 in September 1937, which decreed the gradual adoption of the official Kokuritsu/Kunrei-shiki Romanization system ("Romazi") to replace the traditional Hepburn system, triggering domestic controversy and administrative difficulties for U.S. visa and passport control. Other records detail the shifting linguistic landscape in China, where Japanese was increasingly supplanting English in schools and commerce following Japanese military expansion, recommendations of kanji textbooks and dictionaries for American students, and diplomatic misunderstandings arising from Japanese linguistic styles.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note regarding the necessity of recording Chinese characters (kanji) for Japanese names when conducting investigations of Japanese immigrants.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 341 (Hitchcock, Nagasaki, November 30, 1931): consulates need the characters for Japanese names, with Latin-letter pronunciations on one sheet.
subfiles.title: Characters with Which Japanese Names Are Written (Despatch No. 341)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note emphasizing that Japanese names under inquiry must be written in Chinese characters (kanji) rather than the kana syllabary.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 340 (Hitchcock, November 30, 1931) on Sesuke Kisamiki: names under inquiry need kanji, not kana.
subfiles.title: Japanese Names Written in Characters - Sesuke Kisamiki (Despatch No. 340)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note and attached consular report extract regarding a Japanese scholar's visit to Turkey to study the Latin alphabet reform and possible adoption of Latin characters in Japan.
subfiles.from: American Consulate General, Istanbul (Charles E. Allen)
subfiles.summary: Istanbul consul Allen reports Japanese savant Y. Hoshino studying Turkey's alphabet reform; Japanese find their script inadequate for technical terms and consider adopting Latin letters, with ironic consular remarks.
subfiles.title: Adoption of the Latin Alphabet - Japan (Report from Istanbul)

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting that proficiency in the Japanese language was becoming more valued and prevalent than English in North China.
subfiles.summary: Tsingtao consul Sokobin reports Japanese displacing English in prestige; many city officials were Japan-educated, and an enclosed article describes mushrooming Japanese night schools and declining English classes under Sino-Japanese economic cooperation.
subfiles.title: Proficiency in Japanese Language Now Considered More Important Than Knowledge of English (Despatch No. 417)

subfiles.about: Letter from a former consular officer inquiring about practical textbook recommendations for studying Japanese kanji characters.
subfiles.summary: Edwin Wagstaff of Portland, a former Shanghai consular employee studying Japanese at the YMCA, asks Hornbeck to recommend a practical, alphabetically arranged kanji textbook with Japanese and English definitions.
subfiles.title: Japanese Language Study Inquiry (Letter from Edwin Wagstaff)
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck (Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs)

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum recommending that Wagstaff's inquiry regarding Japanese language textbooks be referred to the American Embassy in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Memo on Wagstaff's inquiry: Mr. Graves had nothing and suggested Denzel Carr in New Haven; it recommends referring the inquiry to the Tokyo Embassy.
subfiles.title: Reference of Japanese Study Inquiry to Tokyo Embassy (Memorandum)

subfiles.about: Letter informing Wagstaff that his request for Japanese textbook recommendations has been referred to the American Embassy in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck (Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck tells Wagstaff the Department lacks the information on kanji textbooks, has forwarded his May 28, 1937 inquiry to Tokyo, and will pass on the reply.
subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Japanese Language Study Inquiry (Letter to Edwin Wagstaff)

subfiles.about: Diplomatic instruction requesting the American Embassy in Tokyo to provide reference book recommendations for Edwin Wagstaff's Japanese language study.
subfiles.summary: Instruction 1271 to Tokyo quotes Wagstaff's request for a concise kanji textbook tied to English translations and asks the Embassy to supply information for a reply.
subfiles.title: Inquiry on Japanese Language Textbooks (Instruction No. 1271)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch providing detailed recommendations of textbooks and dictionaries for English-speaking students of the Japanese language and kanji.
subfiles.summary: Grew recommends the Vaccaris' "Japanese Conversation-Grammar" as the best textbook, plus Sanseido's, Inouye's and Rose-Innes's dictionaries, the last for identifying characters independent of sound.
subfiles.title: Reference Books for Japanese Study (Despatch No. 2507)

subfiles.about: Letter transmitting to Wagstaff the comprehensive textbook and dictionary recommendations prepared by the American Embassy in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck (for the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck passes Wagstaff the Tokyo Embassy's recommendations, with prices and publishers for Vaccari's grammar and the Sanseido, Inouye and Rose-Innes dictionaries.
subfiles.title: Recommendations of Reference Books for Japanese Study (Letter to Edwin Wagstaff)

subfiles.about: Memorandum summarizing Tokyo Consulate General's Despatch No. 72 on the newly decreed official Romanization system and passport documentation issues.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Tokyo despatch 72 of November 12, 1937: Japan is gradually adopting a new romanization altering name spellings on maps, which complicates immigration and consular records and prompted talks with the Foreign Office on passports.
subfiles.title: Adoption of New System of Transliteration of Japanese Words (Memorandum)

subfiles.about: Detailed consular report on Cabinet Order No. 3 decreeing the official Kokuritsu/Kunrei Romanization system, its divergence from the Hepburn system, and consular procedures for passport and visa records.
subfiles.from: American Consulate General, Tokyo (C. R. Cameron)
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 72 from American Consul General C. R. Cameron in Tokyo reports on Japanese Cabinet Order No. 3 of September 21, 1937, promulgated by Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe, mandating the gradual substitution of the Hepburn Romanization system with an official national system (Kunrei-shiki). Cameron explains the spelling divergences across 21 syllables and discusses informal conferences held between Vice Consul Charles A. Cooper and Akira Fukuoka of the Japanese Foreign Office, who gave assurances that former spellings would be retained on passports for previous holders. Cameron recommends that U.S. consulates adopt double-indexing of names and enter former spellings in parentheses on visas and transit certificates, enclosing a clipping of Cabinet Order No. 3 from the Official Gazette, an English translation, and a comparative syllabary chart.
subfiles.title: New System of Romanization (Romaji) for the Japanese Language (Despatch No. 72)

subfiles.about: Consular despatch reporting on the practical rollout of official Romaji, commercial and public reactions, and Diet debates over its non-obligatory status.
subfiles.from: American Consulate General, Tokyo (C. R. Cameron)
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 176 from American Consul General C. R. Cameron at Tokyo reviews the increasing introduction of the official Romaji system by government agencies, the Japan Tourist Bureau, commercial advertisements, and NYK liners like the S.S. Chichibu Maru (Titibu Maru). Cameron reports on growing public criticism and an interpellation in the Imperial Diet, where the Education Minister clarified that while the system was adopted for official textbooks and recommended to government departments, its general use was not compulsory. The despatch encloses a printed protest letter from Ikunoshin Kadono, President of the Romaji Hirome Kai, addressed to Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe, and is preserved in the file in triplicate copies (pages 32-33, 34-35, and 36-37).
subfiles.title: Increasing Use of Official Romaji (Despatch No. 176)

subfiles.about: Military intelligence report analyzing the adoption of the official "Romazi" system, phonetics tables, and public controversy in Japan.
subfiles.from: Military Attaché, Tokyo (Major Harry I. T. Creswell)
subfiles.summary: G-2 Report 9450 by Major Creswell analyzes Japan's uniform "Romazi" system, with a table against Hepburn and press controversy; confusion led the liner Chichibu Maru to revert from "Titubu."
subfiles.title: Change in Romanization System (G-2 Report No. 9450)
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note regarding a report on the mandatory teaching of the Japanese language in primary schools in Peiping, China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Lockhart's February 1939 report: Japanese became a required subject in Peiping primary schools under the Japanese-sponsored regime.
subfiles.title: Teaching of Japanese in Chinese Schools (Report by Lockhart)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for Telegram No. 661 concerning representations to the Japanese Foreign Minister regarding the July 7, 1940 Shanghai incident and linguistic misunderstandings.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo / Japan (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Telegram 661 (August 3, 1940): Grew told Japan's Foreign Minister, who blamed language differences for a Shanghai Marine-gendarme incident, the expressions used were too definite to minimize.
subfiles.title: Incident of July 7, 1940, at Shanghai and Language Misunderstandings (Telegram No. 661)
